Bernhardt et al. 2020, CDBME 6(3):139-142: abstract and metadata only (Crossref and DOAJ REST APIs); the full text on degruyter.com / degruyterbrill.com (empty HTTP 202 bot challenge), db-thueringen.de (proof-of-work page), core.ac.uk and doaj.org article page (HTTP 403) could not be opened
evidence_location: Fiedler 2014 Table 1 'Electrode design parameters' (row 'approx. electrode contact surface (mm2)': Ti/TiN 3.5, PU/TiN 85.1, Au 6, Ag/AgCl 42.5; pin number 1, 24, 15; pin height 2.5, 6, 3 mm), Figure 1 caption (pin shape 'causes a small indentation in the human scalp'), Discussion ('contact surface given in Table 1 was calculated based on the geometry of the pin tips'). Liu 2023 Table A4 (dry contact electrodes): 'Multipin shaped electrode <200 kΩ (forehead); <600 kΩ (occipital) [41]', 'Multipin dry EEG electrodes 101–102 kΩ [40]', 'Active comb-shaped dry electrodes 102 kΩ [83,84]', 'Flexible dry PU/TiN-multipin electrodes 72–125 kΩ [90]', 'Soft pin-shaped dry electrode with bristles 101–102 kΩ [46]'. Bernhardt 2020 abstract: 'a novel hybrid dual-textile headband comprising multipin and multiwave electrodes'.
quote: approx. electrode contact surface (mm2) 3.5 85.1 6 42.5; Multipin shaped electrode <200 kΩ (forehead); <600 kΩ (occipital)
discrepancy: The four contact areas (85.1 rounded to 85) and the pin counts match Fiedler 2014 Table 1, and the forehead/occiput impedances match Liu 2023 Table A4 verbatim; 'tens of kilohms to about 600 kΩ' is a fair summary of the multipin and comb rows (Liu prints the ranges as '101–102 kΩ' and '102 kΩ', evidently 10^1–10^2 and 10^2 kΩ with superscripts lost; 72–125 kΩ for the PU/TiN multipin). Two nuances: (1) Fiedler attributes the scalp indentation to the pin shape of all three dry designs (Figure 1 caption), not specifically to the polyurethane electrode, and states the areas are nominal values computed from pin-tip geometry with actual contact varying with hair density and contact pressure. (2) The three Bernhardt-sourced statements (forehead and mastoid free of dense hair, a flat or wave-shaped contact touching over its face, wet gel bridging hair) could not be checked: only the abstract was reachable, which confirms a headband with multipin and multiwave electrodes but none of those sentences.
suggested_fix: '...85 mm² for a soft 24-pin polyurethane electrode (the pins of all three dry designs indent the scalp slightly); these are nominal areas computed from the pin-tip geometry, and the actual contact varies with hair density and pressure...'. Keep the forehead/mastoid and gel sentences flagged as unverified until the Bernhardt full text has been read.

checked_sources: Ishii et al. 2014, Front Hum Neurosci 8:406: full text XML from Europe PMC (PMC4052629)
Gärtner et al. 2015, Front Behav Neurosci 9:96: full text XML from Europe PMC (PMC4403551)
Friedrich et al. 2013, Clin Neurophysiol 124(5):916-927: abstract only (Europe PMC record 23290926; full text paywalled)
Scherer et al. 2015, PLoS ONE 10(5):e0123727: full text XML from Europe PMC (PMC4436356)
evidence_location: Ishii 2014 Introduction, first sentence ('a distinct train of focal 5–7 Hz theta waves which appears over medial frontal areas ... when performing a broad range of cognitive tasks demanding mental concentration'), Abstract ('Fmθ during mental calculation is generated in the dorsal anterior cingulate and adjacent medial prefrontal cortex'), Table 1 (theta ERS in medial prefrontal BA 8/9 and right anterior cingulate BA 32; MEG beamformer during mental subtraction). Gärtner 2015 Abstract and Discussion ('late-onset, sustained FMT increases during mental arithmetic'; FMT defined there as 4–8 Hz). Friedrich 2013 Abstract: Methods ('Fourteen able-bodied users participated in 10 sessions, plus a follow-up session ... word association, mental subtraction, spatial navigation, and motor imagery') and Results. Scherer 2015 Abstract ('brain-teaser' = mental subtraction and word association; 'dynamic imagery' = hand and feet MI), Introduction ('mental tasks activate spatially distinct cortical areas'), Results (SUB vs FEET highest, median GMAC ≥ 77% both days; WORD vs HAND, SUB vs HAND, WORD vs FEET ≥ 70%; HAND vs FEET worst, ≤ 64%; nine users with stroke or spinal cord injury, offline 10x10-fold simulation).
quote: Eight users reached mean accuracies of 61-72% and managed to control all 4 classes above chance in single-sessions.
discrepancy: All numbers check out (8 of 14, 61–72%, four tasks, 10 weeks, brain-teaser plus dynamic imagery pairs best in end-users with disability). One task in the claim is not in any cited source: 'mental rotation' does not occur in Ishii, Gärtner or Scherer (full texts) nor in the Friedrich 2013 abstract (tasks: word association, mental subtraction, spatial navigation, motor imagery; Scherer: WORD, SUB, NAV, HAND, FEET); it belongs to the group's earlier uncited work. Minor nuances dropped: Friedrich's eight users controlled all four classes 'above chance in single-sessions', and the stability over 10 weeks refers to a follow-up session 'without training'; Ishii's source localisation is MEG during mental subtraction; Scherer's end-user result is an offline simulation in nine users (SUB vs FEET best, HAND vs FEET worst).
suggested_fix: Drop 'and mental rotation' (or cite the study that used it). Optionally: '8 of 14 users reached mean accuracies of 61–72% and controlled all four classes above chance within single sessions, with performance and brain patterns stable at a follow-up ten weeks later without training'.
bibliographic_issues: None found. All four records match Europe PMC: Front Hum Neurosci 8:406 (2014); Front Behav Neurosci 9:96 (2015); Clin Neurophysiol 124(5):916-927 (2013); PLoS One 10(5):e0123727 (2015).

checked_sources: Birbaumer et al. 2003, IEEE TNSRE 11(2):120-123: abstract only (Europe PMC record 12899251; full text paywalled; the pure.mpg.de repository copy sits behind an Anubis proof-of-work bot check and was not opened)

Birbaumer et al. 1999, Nature 398:297-298: nature.com preview paragraph only (the page shows the first paragraph then 'preview of subscription content'; the PDF URL returned HTTP 429); no abstract exists in Europe PMC
Not a cited source, seen for context only: Kübler et al. 1999, Exp Brain Res 124:223-232 (open PDF at kops.uni-konstanz.de), the same group's full description of the Thought Translation Device
evidence_location: Birbaumer 2003 abstract: 'self-regulation of SCPs is learned through visual-auditory feedback and positive reinforcement of SCPs; during the spelling phase, patients select letters or words with their SCPs'; 'Results showed involvement of basal ganglia and premotor cortex for required SCP positivity'; 'clinical outcome of 11 paralyzed patients'. Birbaumer 1999 preview: 'a new means of communication for the completely paralysed that uses slow cortical potentials (SCPs) of the electro-encephalogram to drive an electronic spelling device'.
quote: Results showed involvement of basal ganglia and premotor cortex for required SCP positivity.
discrepancy: Supported by the accessible text: operant feedback training of SCPs with the Thought Translation Device, spelling by completely paralysed patients, and the fMRI finding (basal ganglia and premotor cortex for required positivity). Not found in any accessible text of the two cited sources: recording at the vertex, 'lasting seconds', 'over weeks to months', 'trials of a few seconds', 'about two characters per minute' and 'about seven trials per character with the full alphabet'. For orientation, the uncited Kübler et al. 1999 paper states: SCP at Cz (vertex) produced in a 2-s rhythm within 4-s trials; training 'for several months', 'more than 100 sessions'; the dichotomic speller needs 5 levels for 32 symbols and 'the mean number of trials per letter is 23.95' at 20% error rates. That conflicts with 'about seven trials per character' unless the figure assumes near-perfect accuracy (five selections minimum), and the two-characters-per-minute rate was not seen anywhere.
suggested_fix: Either open the Nature letter's full text and confirm the rate and trials-per-character figures there, or move the timing and rate numbers to the paper that states them (Kübler et al. 1999 for 2-s/4-s trials, five binary selections for a 32-symbol alphabet and months of training). Safe rewording from what is verified: 'patients learned by operant feedback to make their SCP more positive or more negative on command and used it to select letters; fMRI implicated the basal ganglia and premotor cortex in the required positivity'.
bibliographic_issues: None found. Nature 398(6725):297-298, issue date 25 March 1999, doi:10.1038/18581 (nature.com and Europe PMC); IEEE Trans Neural Syst Rehabil Eng 11(2):120-123 (2003), doi:10.1109/TNSRE.2003.814439 (Europe PMC).

checked_sources: Treder et al. 2011, J NeuroEng Rehabil 8:24: full text XML from Europe PMC (PMC3114715)
van Gerven and Jensen 2009, J Neurosci Methods 179(1):78-84: abstract only (Europe PMC record 19428515; full text paywalled, no open copy found)
evidence_location: Treder 2011 Abstract (Results: 'prolonged alpha synchronization over posterior electrode sites (PO and O electrodes)'; 'Mean accuracy for the best-classifiable pair amounted to 74.6%'), Results/Classification ('Mean accuracy for the best pair of directions was 74.6% ± 2.3%', electrodes PO3,4,7-10 and Oz,1,2, 8–12 Hz, 500–2000 ms; 'We focused only on alpha synchronization, because the preceding alpha desynchronization did not show distinctive patterns for the different directions'), Figure 3 (eight participants, fifteen direction pairs), Discussion. Methods: N = 8, strict fixation of a central dot, six cued directions. van Gerven 2009 abstract: MEG, 15 subjects, covert attention left/right/up/down for 2500 ms, SVM, 'up to a maximum of 69% correctly classified trials (25% chance level)', 'promising as a control signal for a two-dimensional BCI'.
quote: prolonged alpha synchronization over posterior electrode sites (PO and O electrodes) ... best-classifiable pair amounted to 74.6%
discrepancy: The 74.6% figure, the parieto-occipital sites, eyes fixated, single-trial classification and the two-dimensional control proposal are all supported. Not supported by the accessible texts: the direction of the change. Neither Treder nor the van Gerven abstract says alpha 'falls over the hemisphere contralateral to the attended side'; Treder found an early alpha desynchronization without direction-specific patterns and classified the subsequent alpha increase (synchronization, 500–2000 ms) whose topography differed by direction ('ipsilateral' never occurs; 'contralateral' appears only in a left-hemisphere-dominance analysis). Nuances: 74.6% ± 2.3% is the mean over 8 participants of each one's best pair among six directions (15 pairs), the best pair varying across participants (mostly some left-versus-right combination); van Gerven and Jensen 2009 is an MEG study (15 subjects, four directions, up to 69% correct), not scalp EEG.
suggested_fix: 'Covert shifts of visual attention, with the eyes fixated, modulate alpha power over parieto-occipital cortex with a topography that depends on the attended direction (in one EEG study a sustained alpha increase over PO and O electrodes); the change is classifiable on single trials, with a mean accuracy of 74.6% for each participant's best pair of six directions (8 participants), and modulation of posterior alpha by attention in two dimensions has been proposed, from MEG data (four directions classified up to 69%), as a control signal.' If the contralateral-decrease wording is kept, cite a source that reports it (Treder cites Worden et al. 2000, J Neurosci 20:RC63, for retinotopic alpha increases over occipital cortex) after checking it.
bibliographic_issues: None found. J Neuroeng Rehabil 8:24 (2011), doi:10.1186/1743-0003-8-24; J Neurosci Methods 179(1):78-84 (2009), doi:10.1016/j.jneumeth.2009.01.016, both matching Europe PMC.
